newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian raw sugar imports to slow soon - trade.
newsitem.headline: Russian raw sugar imports to slow soon - trade.

text.p: Russia's imports of raw sugar are expected to slow by early August as refiners turn their attention to the domestic beet crop, industry sources said on Monday.
Raw sugar imports rose over the past three months after running well behind year-ago levels in the first quarter of the year, but the overall 1997 volume is still expected to lag last year's.
"I would expect sugar imports, particularly raws, to drop quite sharply after the start of August as Russian refineries work on their own beets," said a London-based sugar analyst.
"The period of higher imports is almost at an end."
The area sown to beets this year was around 930,000 hectares, down 12-13 percent from 1996 levels and the lowest level in over 40 years.
Output is forecast at a paltry 15-17 million tonnes, little changed from 16.1 million tonnes in 1996 and comfortably shy of the official target of 22 million.
Russia's annual beet crop averaged over 33 million tonnes in the late 1980s, State Statistics Committee figures show.

"We are looking for a sugar crop of somewhere between 16 and 17 million tonnes, well short of the government's target," said Alexander Netyosov, deputy general director of the Rossakhsvyokla producers' group.
"Conditions for the crop at the moment look very favourable. Last year they were much worse, so even with a smaller area we can catch up."
A senior Western trader said the beet harvest should yield between 1.7 to 2.0 million tonnes of refined sugar. He pegged Russia's annual white sugar demand at 4.6-4.7 million tonnes.
Official figures show Russian imported 1.70 million tonnes of raws and 1.44 tonnes of refined sugar in 1996, but traders and analysts said the overall total this year would be down.
"Total imports this year are likely to be down on last year, because Russian imported too much sugar in 1996 and so there was excess stock at the start of this year," the trader said.
He forecast total sugar imports at around 3.0 million tonnes, above the analyst's forecast of 2.6 to 2.7 million.
The trader said imports had risen in the second quarter and in July but that this was a normal seasonal pattern.
"Imports are likely to reach a peak in June or July -- it's a seasonal thing -- the peak period for demand."

Imports of white sugar from Ukraine, which dominates the Russian import market, could be under pressure this year as a result of a new 25 percent duty on white sugar imports implemented by Russia in May.
But a sharply higher crop and the lack of alternative markets could force Kiev's hand and limit the impact of the duty, another trader said.
"Ukraine have had a very good crop, so even with this duty they have to find a home for their sugar somewhere," he said.
Ukrainian officials forecast last week a sugar beet crop of 30 to 31 million tonnes in 1997, up from 24 million in 1996.
"When the Russian crop starts to come in, then if anything it will be whites that are imported, not raws, as refineries will be working on home-grown sugar," the analyst said.
Cuba accounts for the bulk of Russian raw sugar imports, although volumes are now brought in mostly privately rather than under Soviet-era sugar-for-oil barter deals.

This trend could continue despite a new intergovernmental deal signed in June, because recent experience shows the deals are only partially carried out, a trader at a Russian firm active in recent protocols said.

Russia would buy 3.25 million tonnes of Cuban raws in exchange for sending Havana 9.75 million tonnes of oil under the latest deal. The total included volumes not yet traded under the 1996 agreement, and covered 1997 and 1998, the trader added.
--Mike Collett-White, Moscow Newsroom +7095 941 8520
